en: Warm waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate and rise, forming massive rotating clouds that develop into typhoons.
Tiny coral polyps in the Tubbataha Reefs extract calcium from seawater to build hard limestone structures over centuries.
Rainwater seeps into the limestone of St. Paul Mountain, slowly dissolving the rock to carve the Puerto Princesa Underground River.
Tectonic forces uplifted ancient coral reefs in Bohol, and rainwater erosion subsequently sculpted the limestone into conical Chocolate Hills.
Underground magma in Albay heats groundwater into steam, which rises to spin turbines and generate electricity at the Tiwi power plant.
Dense mangrove roots in Olango Island trap sediment and break ocean wave energy, which prevents coastal soil erosion.
Repeated eruptions of thick, sticky lava from Mayon Volcano pile up around the vent, creating its perfectly symmetrical cone shape.
The Cagayan River drops its carried sediment into the Babuyan Channel where the water slows down, forming a fertile river delta.
Carving step-like flat areas into mountainsides creates the Banaue Rice Terraces, which slow rainwater runoff and prevent severe soil erosion.
The Habagat monsoon pushes moisture from the West Philippine Sea toward Luzon, causing heavy rainfall on the western coasts during summer.
Past eruptions of Mount Pinatubo deposited thick volcanic ash, which slowly weathers into mineral-rich soil that makes central Luzon highly fertile.
The collision of the Eurasian and Philippine Sea tectonic plates pushes the Earth's crust upward, forming the rugged Cordillera mountain range.
